accepted.question_text: Does every closed Riemannian manifold contain a closed geodesic multinet that does not contain any non-trivial periodic geodesic? Here "closed" means there are no unbalanced (boundary) vertices, and a geodesic multinet is the version of a geodesic net that allows edge multiplicities and self-intersections.

evidence.quote: Problem 2.0.1. Is it true that each closed Riemannian manifold contains a closed geodesic multinet not containing a non-trivial periodic geodesic?

accepted.question_text: Which 3-regular graphs G occur as the underlying graph of a closed geodesic net on the round 3-sphere? Here a closed geodesic net is a geodesic net with no unbalanced vertices.

evidence.quote: Problem 2.0.2. Classify all 3-regular graphs G such that the round 3-sphere has a geodesic net modelled on G.

accepted.question_text: Does every closed Riemannian manifold of dimension >= 3 admit a closed geodesic net whose underlying graph is a theta-graph, namely a graph with two vertices joined by three distinct edges?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.0.3. Is it true that each closed Riemannian manifold of dimension ≥ 3 has a θ-graph shaped closed geodesic net?

accepted.question_text: For a fixed closed Riemannian manifold M, is there a function f_M, depending on the geometry and topology of M, such that every closed geodesic net on M of length L has at most f_M(L) balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Problem 2.0.4 (Becker-Kahn). Let M be a closed Riemannian manifold. Is there a function fM (depending on geometry and topology of M) such that each closed geodesic net on M of length L has at most fM(L) (balanced) vertices?

accepted.question_text: Let Sigma be the set of all triples S of points in the Euclidean plane for which there exist geodesic multinets with exactly three unbalanced vertices located at S and with arbitrarily many balanced vertices. Is Sigma a measure-zero subset of (R^2)^3?

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1.3. Let Σ be the set of all triples S of points of the Euclidean plane such that there exist geodesic multinets with 3 unbalanced vertices at S and arbitrarily many balanced vertices. Is it true that Σ is a set of measure zero (in (R2)3)?

accepted.question_text: Is there a function f(n) such that every geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane with three boundary (unbalanced) vertices and with multiplicity of every edge at most n has at most f(n) balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1.4. Is there a function f (n) such that for each geodesic multinet with three boundary vertices in the Euclidean plane such the that multiplicities of all edges do not exceed n the number of balanced vertices does not exceed f (n)?

accepted.question_text: Classify all geodesic multinets in the Euclidean plane that have exactly three unbalanced vertices.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.1.5. Classify all geodesic multinets in the Euclidean plane with 3 unbalanced vertices.

accepted.question_text: Either construct an irreducible geodesic net in the Euclidean plane with four unbalanced vertices and more than 16 balanced vertices, or prove that no such geodesic net exists. Here irreducible means that no proper subset of its edges, together with the incident vertices, is itself a geodesic net with the same set of unbalanced vertices.

evidence.quote: Problem 3.2.1. Find an irreducible geodesic net with 4 unbalanced vertices in the Euclidean plane with more than 16 balanced vertices (or prove that such a geodesic net does not exist.)

one can define irreducible geodesic nets on a given set S of unbalanced vertices as geodesic nets such that no subgraph formed by a proper subset of the set of edges (with all incident vertices) is a geodesic net with the same set S of unbalanced vertices.

accepted.question_text: Do there exist geodesic nets in the Euclidean plane with exactly four unbalanced vertices and arbitrarily many balanced vertices? The conjecture further suggests that this may already hold when the four unbalanced vertices are the vertices of a square.
accepted.context_brief: Arbitrarily many balanced vertices from four boundary points

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.2.2. There exist geodesic nets in the Euclidean plane with 4 unbalanced vertices and an arbitrarily large number of balanced vertices. (Moreover, we will not be surprised if this assertion is already true in the case when the set of unbalanced vertices coincides with the set of vertices of a square).

accepted.question_text: Is there a number N such that every irreducible geodesic net whose unbalanced vertices are exactly the four vertices of a regular tetrahedron has at most N balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Problem 3.2.3. Is there a number N such that each irreducible geodesic net with unbalanced vertices at all vertices of a regular tetrahedron has at most N balanced vertices?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an integer N0 and an N0-tuple S of points in the Euclidean plane such that, for every N, there is a geodesic net whose set of unbalanced vertices is exactly S and whose number of balanced vertices is greater than N? Moreover, do such N0-tuples S form a subset of (R^2)^N0 of positive measure, or even a non-empty open subset?
accepted.context_brief: Fixed boundary set with unbounded complexity

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.3.1. 1. There exist N0 and an N0-tuple S such that for each N there exists a geodesic net with S being its set of unbalanced vertices and the number of balanced vertices greater than N. 2. Furthermore, there exist not merely one such N0-tuple S but a subset of (R2 )N0 of positive measure (or even a non-empty open subset) of such N0-tuples.

accepted.question_text: Can the number of balanced vertices of a geodesic net in the Euclidean plane be bounded above by a function of only two quantities: the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance? Here the total imbalance is the sum, over all unbalanced vertices, of the norms of their imbalance vectors.

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.4.1 (M. Gromov). The number of balanced vertices of a geodesic net in the Euclidean plane can be bounded above in terms of the number of unbalanced vertices and the total imbalance.
The sum of imbalances ∑v∈S imb(v) over the set of all unbalanced points is called the total imbalance of the geodesic net.

accepted.question_text: Is there a function f such that every geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane with n unbalanced vertices, diameter D, and total length L has fewer than f(L/D, n) balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3.4.2. There exists a function f of such that each geodesic multinet in the Euclidean plane with n unbalanced vertices, diameter D, and total length L has less than f (L/D, n) balanced vertices.

accepted.question_text: Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. Does there exist a function f_M, invariant under rescaling of M, with the following property: whenever a geodesic net G on M has total length L, adjusted length L_tilde, diameter D, and n unbalanced vertices, the number of balanced vertices is at most f_M(L_tilde, L/D, n)? Here the adjusted length L_tilde is obtained by summing over all edges e_i the arclength integral of 1 / inj(e_i(s)), where inj(e_i(s)) is the injectivity radius of M at the point e_i(s). In particular, if M has injectivity radius inj > 0, must the number of balanced vertices be at most f_M(L / inj, L / D, n)?

evidence.quote: The adjusted total length L̃ of a geodesic net is the sum of integrals over all edges ei parametrized by their respective arclengths of 1 / inj(ei(s)), where inj(ei(s)) denotes the injectivity radius of the ambient Riemannian manifold at ei(s).

Conjecture 3.4.3 (Boundedness conjecture for geodesic nets on Riemannian manifolds). Let M be a complete Riemannian manifold. There exists a function fM which depends on M but is invariant with respect to rescalings of M with the following property: Let G be a geodesic net on M with total length L, adjusted length L̃ and diameter D that has n unbalanced vertices. Then its number of balanced vertices does not exceed fM (L̃, L / D, n). In particular, if M has injectivity radius inj > 0, then the number of balanced vertices does not exceed fM (L / inj, L / D, n).

accepted.question_text: Consider the layered geodesic-net construction G_n(phi) built from seven equally spaced outer vertices, an inner seven-vertex layer determined by a deviation parameter phi, and subsequent layers V_i produced by the paper's suspension-and-winging rules. For odd i, define the suspension angle phi_i(phi) as the angle OPv between the ray from the center O of the outer circle to the relevant hook P and the segment Pv for a vertex v in V_i. For even i, define phi_i(phi) as the angle OXv, where X is the third vertex of the equilateral triangle on the relevant outer pair P,Q and v lies in V_i. Does the derivative sequence phi_i'(0) ever repeat, or is it nonrepeating for all i?

evidence.quote: Definition 4.5.1 (Suspension angle for one-hook suspensions, layers Vi for i odd). Whenever we do a one-hook suspension for a layer Vi, we are connecting a vertex v to the closest vertex on the outer circle. Denote the center of the outer circle by O and the hook by P. Then we define the suspension angle ϕi to be the angle ∠OPv.

Definition 4.5.2 (Suspension angle for two-hook suspensions, layers Vi for i even). Whenever we do a two-hook suspension for a layer Vi, we are connecting a vertex v to the closest two vertices on the outer circle P and Q through the Fermat point of ΔPvQ. As before, we denote by X the third vertex of the equilateral triangle ΔPQX used for the construction of the Fermat point. Let O be the center of the outer circle. Then we define the suspension angle ϕi to be the angle ∠OXv.
Conjecture 4.5.7. ϕ′i (0) is a sequence that never repeats itself.

accepted.question_text: In the same layered construction G_n(phi), is it true that for sufficiently small nonzero phi the finite sequence of suspension angles phi_0(phi), phi_1(phi), ..., phi_n(phi) never repeats a value? Equivalently, does this force G_n(phi) to be a geodesic net in which all edges have weight one, while still having 14 unbalanced vertices and, for large n, arbitrarily many balanced vertices?

evidence.quote: Lemma 4.5.5. If for any fixed ϕ ∈ (−ϵ, ϵ), the sequence ϕi(ϕ) never repeats itself, all edges of the resulting geodesic net Gn(ϕ) intersect transversally (if at all). In other words, there are no edges with weight other than one.

Conjecture 4.5.8. For small nonzero ϕ ∈ (−ϵ, ϵ), the sequence ϕi (ϕ) never repeats itself. This implies that Gn (ϕ) is a geodesic net for which all edges have weight one. So this Gn (ϕ) would in fact fulfill all required conditions: (a) There are 14 unbalanced vertices. (b) For n large enough, we can achieve an arbitrarily large number of balanced vertices. (c) All edges have weight one.
